title: Launch out into the deep (Luke 5:1–11)
hook: Peter has fished all night for nothing and lets down the nets once more

segments.voice: Yesterday, forty days hungry in the desert, and three refusals. Your line was not by bread alone. What were you really hungry for? Day thirty-four.

Dawn on the Lake of Galilee. Two boats pulled up on the shore. The fishermen are out of them, washing their nets, which is what you do after a long night. And it has been a long night. Simon and his partners have worked from dark to dawn and caught nothing. Not a small catch. Nothing. You know this feeling: the shift that went nowhere, the job applications with no reply, the effort with nothing to show. They're tired, and they want to go home. Then a crowd arrives, pressing around a teacher, and the teacher steps into Simon's boat. Today: what happens when you're asked to try once more.
screen: `ALL NIGHT, NOTHING.` → `WASHING THE EMPTY NETS.` → `A TEACHER STEPS INTO THE BOAT.`

segments.voice: Jesus asks Simon to push out a little from the land, and he teaches the crowd sitting in the boat. Then, when he's finished, he turns to Simon and says, in the Douay-Rheims: "Launch out into the deep, and let down your nets for a draught." Simon is the expert here. He knows the lake. He knows that on this lake you fish at night, and he's just done that, for hours. His answer is honest, and a little tired: "Master, we have laboured all the night, and have taken nothing: but at thy word I will let down the net." That word but is the hinge. Not because I think it'll work. Because you said so. And the nets fill so full they start to break. They wave to their partners in the other boat, James and John, and both boats fill until they begin to sink. Now look at Simon. He doesn't celebrate. He falls down at Jesus's knees and says: depart from me, for I am a sinful man. The catch has frightened him, not with danger, but with nearness. And Jesus answers: fear not, from now on you'll be catching people. They bring the boats to land, leave everything, and follow him. The Catholic Church loves this line. In the Latin Bible it's three short words: duc in altum. Pope John Paul the Second used it to open the new millennium, calling the whole Church to launch out into the deep. Simon, of course, is the one the Church will call Peter.
screen: `LAUNCH OUT INTO THE DEEP.` · `WE TOILED ALL NIGHT. BUT AT THY WORD.` · `NETS BREAKING, BOATS SINKING.` · `DEPART FROM ME. FEAR NOT.` · then, large: `DUC IN ALTUM.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: find one thing you've stopped trying at. Settle and breathe. Let it come to mind: a conversation that never goes well, a habit you keep failing to start, a hope you put down. Don't pick the biggest. Pick one you could try once more today. Hear Simon's sentence, and let it be yours if it fits: I've worked all night and caught nothing, but I'll let down the net. If you pray, you can offer the trying to God. The bell holds the time.
Launch out into the deep. A tired fisherman lets down his nets once more, at someone else's word. Today's word.
screen: `LAUNCH OUT INTO THE DEEP — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: launch out into the deep. Today, try the one thing once more. Not because you're sure. Just once more, a little further out. Day thirty-four.

howItsDone: Catholics hear this Gospel at Sunday Mass in the Lectionary's year of Luke, and "duc in altum" is a much-quoted motto since John Paul II used it in his 2001 letter for the new millennium.

trapdoor: what you thought: a story about a lucky day's fishing.
what it means: a tired expert tries once more at someone else's word, and the catch leaves him on his knees.
what a scholar hears: duc in altum, the Latin line John Paul II chose in 2001 to send the whole Church into a new century.

notes: Douay-Rheims wording of Luke 5:4 and 5:5 given from memory; confirm. The teach screen paraphrases 5:5 as 'we toiled all night' to avoid British spelling in a screen head; confirm acceptable.
'Depart from me, for I am a sinful man' and 'from now on you'll be catching people' (5:8, 5:10) are paraphrased.
The Vulgate of Luke 5:4 reads 'Duc in altum, et laxate retia vestra in capturam'; confirm.
Night fishing as the normal practice on the lake: widely stated; confirm.
John Paul II, Novo Millennio Ineunte (January 6, 2001), opens with and returns to 'Duc in altum'; confirm section numbers.
